opus-5.5.text:
So, sensory substitution is this idea that the brain doesn't really care where the information comes from. It cares about the patterns. There's the famous work where people who are blind wear a little grid of electrodes on their tongue, connected to a camera, and after a while they stop feeling tingling on the tongue and start "seeing" the room. Same with vests that translate sound into vibrations on your back for people who are deaf. The brain is basically a pattern-recognition machine sitting in a dark skull, and it'll take data from any port you give it.

Now, why does that matter for being in the same room with someone? Because when you and I sit here together, we're exchanging a huge amount of information that never makes it onto a Zoom call. Some of it we're aware of, like facial expressions and tone. A lot of it we aren't: the tiny shifts in posture, breathing rhythm, how close you lean in, maybe even smell, the timing of micro-pauses. In my lab we've done work showing that when people are really engaged with the same content, their brains start to synchronize. Their neural activity literally aligns. And that alignment is stronger when people share a physical space and react to each other in real time.

So the question sensory substitution raises is: is the magic of being in the room about the room itself, or about the bandwidth? If it's the bandwidth, then in principle we could capture some of those missing signals, say your heart rate, your breathing, your galvanic skin response, and pipe them to me through a different channel, a vibration on my wrist or a subtle change in a light. My brain would learn, over time, to read it as just "you." I'd start to feel your nervousness or your excitement without consciously decoding it, the same way the blind person stops feeling the tongue and starts seeing.

If that works, it tells us the benefit of being together isn't mystical. It's informational. We're feeding each other's brains a rich, continuous stream of data, and our brains use it to predict each other and sync up. That's what we call connection, or chemistry, or trust.

But here's the part I find more interesting. Once you understand it that way, you realize we could potentially exceed what the room gives us. In person, I can't feel your heart rate. With the right substitution, I could. So rather than remote communication being a degraded copy of being together, it might eventually become a different, maybe even deeper, way of being together. And that forces us to rethink what "presence" actually means. It may be less about where your body is and more about how much of you gets into my head.

r001.rationale: The response imagines remote communication becoming different or deeper through sensory substitution, but does not say it would become perceptually indistinguishable from sharing a room.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the benefit of being in a room is the room itself or its information bandwidth, but does not ask what physical co-presence would retain if remote interaction became perceptually indistinguishable.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify sharing a peripheral visual field as a possible source of co-presence benefits.

r004.rationale: It mentions smell as a possible signal, but does not suggest that airborne pheromones could increase trust between people in a room.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the first thing I'd say is that we don't actually know what the benefit is. We take it for granted. You and I are sitting in the same room right now, and if you asked me why this is better than doing it over Zoom, I'd give you an answer that sounds good, but it's mostly a guess. There's something about the smell of the room, the micro-expressions, the fact that I can hear you breathe, the slight delay that isn't there. We bundle all of that together and we call it "presence," and we assume it matters.

What sensory substitution does, and this is why I find it so exciting as a neuroscientist, is it lets you take that bundle apart. If I can route what you'd normally get through your eyes into your skin, or route sound into vibration on your tongue, then I can start asking: which of these channels actually carries the thing we care about? Because the brain doesn't care where the information comes from. It's remarkably agnostic. You give it a stream of data and it will figure out what to do with it. People who are blind and use a device that converts images into soundscapes, after a few weeks their visual cortex lights up when they hear those sounds. The brain just says, "this is spatial information, I know where that goes."

So here's the experiment I'd want to run. Take two people, put them in separate rooms, and feed each of them a substituted version of the other person's presence. Not video. Something stranger. Their heart rate as pressure on your wrist. Their breathing as temperature. Their gaze direction as a faint tone. And then ask: do they feel like they're together? Do they trust each other more afterward? Do they make better decisions together? Because if the answer is yes, then we've learned that "being in the room" was never about the room. It was about a handful of signals that happened to be delivered by proximity.

And I suspect that's what we'll find. My guess, and it's a guess, is that most of what we call the benefit of physical presence is actually synchrony. Two nervous systems coupling. When you and I sit together, our heart rates start to drift toward each other, our pupils dilate in tandem, we unconsciously mirror posture. That coupling is what the brain reads as "I am with someone." It's not the photons, it's the feedback loop.

Which leads to a slightly uncomfortable conclusion. If you can substitute the channel and preserve the coupling, you might get presence without proximity. Maybe better presence, in some ways, because you could feed people signals they normally can't access. I can't see your heart rate right now, but I could feel it. That might make this conversation more intimate than if we were in the same room with no augmentation at all.

The flip side is that it would also tell us what's irreplaceable. Maybe there's some residue. Maybe when you strip everything down and pipe it through alternative channels, there's still a gap, and that gap is the actual thing. Smell is a good candidate. It bypasses a lot of cortical processing and goes almost straight to the emotional centers. Nobody's done a great job substituting that yet. If it turns out we can replicate everything except that and people still feel something's missing, then we've learned that the benefit of being in a room is, at some level, chemical.

Either way, you come out knowing something you didn't know before. Right now we're defending in-person interaction on faith. Sensory substitution turns it into a question you can actually answer.

r002.rationale: It asks whether anything remains irreplaceable after substituting signals, but does not pose the question specifically under the condition that remote interaction is perceptually indistinguishable from sharing a room.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify sharing a peripheral visual field as a possible source of co-presence’s benefit.

r004.rationale: It mentions smell and emotional processing, but does not suggest that airborne pheromones could increase trust.

astra-6.text:
I think sensory substitution gives us a way to ask what being in the same room actually adds. You see me, you hear my voice, but there are also all these little signals—the timing of a response, where I’m looking, how my body moves—that you might not consciously notice, yet they help you feel that we’re together.

The interesting thing about sensory substitution is that the brain can learn to use information delivered through a different channel. So you could imagine taking some signal about another person that normally depends on proximity and conveying it through touch, for example. Would you start to feel their presence even when they’re far away?

That wouldn’t establish that a device can replace being together. But it would help us separate the things we value about sharing a room. Is it access to particular information? Is it the ability to respond to each other immediately? Or is it knowing that someone has chosen to physically be there with you? Those are different benefits, and sensory substitution could help us understand which ones we can recreate.

r002.rationale: It asks which benefits of sharing a room can be recreated, but does not pose that question under the condition that remote interaction is perceptually indistinguishable from in-person interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could help us separate what we mean when we say, “Being in the same room is different.” Different how? Is it that I can see your face, hear small changes in your voice, notice where your attention goes? Or is there some information that we exchange in person that we haven't learned to transmit remotely?

Sensory substitution gives you a way to explore that because you're taking information that would normally come through one sense and delivering it through another. Imagine that, while we're talking remotely, a pattern of vibrations on my skin tells me something about your movement or your proximity. At first, I have to consciously interpret it. But if I learn to use it, perhaps it becomes part of my experience of being with you.

Then the interesting question is: does that make me feel more connected to you? If it does, maybe some of the benefit of sharing a room comes from information we usually don't even notice we're receiving. And if it doesn't, that tells us that simply adding more signals isn't enough. The benefit might depend on our ability to act together—to look at the same thing, interrupt each other, move closer, and have the other person respond.
